title: Homily I — Not death but falling asleep

edition.locus: Migne, PG 96 (Paris, 1860), Homily I on the Dormition, col. 716 (PDF leaf 399)

source_text: Τί τοίνυν τὸ περὶ σὲ τοῦτο μυστήριον ὀνομάσομεν· θάνατον; ἀλλὰ καὶ φυσικῶς ἡ πανίερος καὶ μακαρία σου ψυχὴ τοῦ πανολβίου καὶ ἀκηράτου σου χωρίζεται σώματος, καὶ τὸ σῶμα τῇ νομίμῳ ταφῇ παραδίδοται, ὅμως οὐκ ἐναπομένει ἐν τῷ θανάτῳ, οὐδ' ὑπὸ τῆς φθορᾶς διαλύεται. Ἧς γὰρ τικτούσης ἀλώβητος ἡ παρθενία μεμένηκε, ταύτης μεθισταμένης ἀδιάλυτον τὸ σῶμα πεφύλακται, καὶ πρὸς κρείττονα καὶ θειοτέραν σκηνὴν μετατίθεται, οὐ διακοπτομένην θανάτῳ, ἀλλ' εἰς ἀπεράντους αἰῶνας αἰώνων διαιωνίζουσαν. Ὥσπερ γὰρ οὗτος ὁ ὁλολαμπὴς καὶ ἀείφωτος ἥλιος ὑπὸ τοῦ σεληνιακοῦ πρὸς μικρὸν κρυπτόμενος σώματος, δοκεῖ μέν πως ἐκλιμπάνειν, καὶ τῷ ζόφῳ καλύπτεσθαι, καὶ τῆς αἴγλης ἀντιλαμβάνειν τὸ σκότος, ὅμως αὐτὸς τοῦ οἰκείου φωτὸς οὐκ ἐξίσταται. Ἔχει δὲ ἐν ἑαυτῷ πηγὴν φωτὸς ἀέναον βρύουσαν, μᾶλλον δὲ αὐτὸς πηγὴ φωτὸς ὑπάρχει ἀνέκλειπτος, ὡς ὁ Κτίσας αὐτὸν Θεὸς διετάξατο. Οὕτω καὶ σὺ ἡ πηγὴ τοῦ ἀληθινοῦ φωτὸς ἡ ἀέναος, ὁ ἀδάπανος τῆς αὐτοζωῆς θησαυρὸς, ἡ δαψιλὴς τῆς εὐλογίας ἀνάβλυσις, ἡ πάντων τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἡμῖν αἰτία καὶ πρόξενος, εἰ καὶ πρός τι χρονικὸν διάστημα καλύπτῃ σωματικῶς τῷ θανάτῳ, ἀλλὰ βρύεις ἀφθόνως ἡμῖν φωτὸς ἀπειρεσίου, καὶ ἀμβροσίας ζωῆς, καὶ τῆς ὄντως μακαριότητος ἀνελλιπῆ, καὶ καθαρὰ, καὶ ἀδαπάνητα νάματα, ποταμοὺς χάριτος, ἰαμάτων πηγὰς, εὐλογίαν ἀέναον. Σὺ γὰρ ὡς μῆλον ἐν τοῖς ξύλοις τοῦ δρυμοῦ ἐξήνθησας, καὶ ὁ καρπός σου γλυκασμὸς ἐν λάρυγγι τῶν πιστῶν. Ἐντεῦθεν οὐ θάνατον τὴν ἱεράν σου μετάστασιν λέξομαι, ἀλλὰ κοίμησιν, ἢ ἐκδημίαν, ἢ ἐνδημίαν εἰπεῖν οἰκειότερον. Ἐκδημοῦσα γὰρ τῶν τοῦ σώματος, ἐνδημεῖς πρὸς τὰ κρείττονα.
pass_a_gloss: What then shall we name this mystery about you: death? But even if naturally (φυσικῶς) your all-holy and blessed soul is separated from your all-blessed (πανόλβιος) and undefiled (ἀκήρατος) body, and the body is handed over to lawful (νομίμῳ) burial (ταφή), nevertheless (ὅμως) it does not remain in death, nor is it dissolved by corruption (φθορά). For of whom, giving birth, the virginity remained unharmed (ἀλώβητος), of her, passing over (μεθισταμένης), the body has been guarded undissolved (ἀδιάλυτον), and is transferred (μετατίθεται) to a better and more divine tent (σκηνή), not cut off (διακοπτομένην) by death, but lasting through (διαιωνίζουσαν) into boundless ages of ages. For just as this wholly bright (ὁλολαμπής) and ever-lit (ἀείφωτος) sun, being hidden for a little by the lunar body, seems somehow to fail, and to be covered by the murk (ζόφος), and darkness to take in exchange the radiance (αἴγλη), yet it itself does not depart from (ἐξίσταται) its own light. And it has in itself a fountain of light ever-flowing (ἀέναον) gushing, rather it itself exists an unfailing (ἀνέκλειπτος) fountain of light, as God who created it appointed. Thus also you, the ever-flowing fountain of the true light, the unspendable (ἀδάπανος) treasure of self-life (αὐτοζωή), the abundant (δαψιλής) upwelling of blessing, the cause (αἰτία) and procurer (πρόξενος) to us of all goods, even if for some time-interval you are covered bodily by death, yet you gush (βρύεις) ungrudgingly (ἀφθόνως) to us unfailing (ἀνελλιπῆ) and pure and inexhaustible streams (νάματα) of boundless light and ambrosial (ἀμβρόσιος) life and of the real blessedness (μακαριότης): rivers of grace, springs of healings (ἰάματα), ever-flowing blessing. For you as an apple tree (μῆλον) among the trees of the thicket (δρυμός) blossomed (ἐξήνθησας), and your fruit sweetness in the throat (λάρυγξ) of the faithful. Hence I will not call your holy removal (μετάστασις) death, but falling asleep (κοίμησις), or departure abroad (ἐκδημία), or more properly (οἰκειότερον) to say being at home (ἐνδημία). For being away from home (ἐκδημοῦσα) from the things of the body, you are at home (ἐνδημεῖς) toward the better things.
pass_b_english: What, then, shall we call this mystery that concerns you? Death? Yet even though your all-holy and blessed soul is parted from your most blessed and spotless body, as nature requires, and the body is given over to lawful burial, still it does not remain in death, nor is it dissolved by corruption. For she whose virginity remained unharmed in giving birth has had her body kept undissolved in her passing over, and it is moved to a better and more divine dwelling, not cut short by death, but lasting through endless ages of ages.

For this all-shining, ever-bright sun, when it is hidden for a little while by the body of the moon, seems in some way to fail, to be covered in gloom, and to have its brilliance traded for darkness; yet it does not lose its own light. It has within itself an ever-flowing fountain of light; or rather, it is itself a fountain of light that never fails, as God who created it ordained. So it is with you too, the ever-flowing fountain of the true light, the unspent treasury of Life itself, the rich upwelling of blessing, the cause and provider of every good thing for us. Even if for a space of time you are covered by death in the body, you still pour out for us freely unfailing, pure and inexhaustible streams of boundless light, of immortal life and of true blessedness: rivers of grace, fountains of healing, never-ending blessing. For you have blossomed like an apple tree among the trees of the forest, and your fruit is sweet in the mouths of the faithful (Song of Songs 2:3).

Therefore I will not call your holy passing death, but falling asleep, or departure, or, more fittingly, homecoming. For as you leave the things of the body, you come home to better things (2 Corinthians 5:8).

choices.note: Margin prints Song 2:7; the apple tree among the trees of the forest and the sweet fruit is Song of Songs 2:3, cited.
The Song speaks of the beloved man;
John applies it to Mary. 2 Corinthians 5:8 underlies the ἐκδημία / ἐνδημία pair ('away from the body and at home with the Lord'); rendered 'departure ... homecoming' and 'leave ... come home'.
'The true light' may echo John 1:9; uncertain as a reference, uncited.
The eclipse comparison is kept in full.
πολύφωτος ('full of light') for ἀείφωτος ('ever-bright'); same sense.
